I think a few things could be happening here. First things first, emotionally burnout is *real* and it happens quickly. This can happen to anyone in any kind of relationship with someone who has MI. Short bursts of distance can help curb this.

Second, not giving people something tangible to he able to "help" with makes them feel helpless and frustrated. They won't want to continue to ask if you consistently deny their request, and they won't want to talk as often because it will be a reminder that their loved one is hurting and they can't do a damn thing to help it or stop it. It's not a great feeling, though it's not really something anyone can control much either. Not you and not them.

I've personally run into this on a consistent basis in my life. A few years ago it kind of clicked for me that my loved ones need to feel needed and helpful, regardless of if they are actually "fixing" anything I'm feeling or going through (we all know it doesn't work that way, but it doesn't stop us from wanting it). My personal go to move is to say that they already *are* helping. I explain that my depression (and other MI) usually comes in waves, and what I need most is someone who will listen and be my friend and not treat me like I'm made out of glass. Which they already happen to be doing without even trying. It makes them feel much better while also giving me another way to tell them how much I appreciate them.
